uncited: Early work, such as DS-NeRF, demonstrated that sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) keypoints could serve as effective geometric constraints, significantly reducing the number of training iterations required for convergence [8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md].

Subsequent research expanded this to include monocular depth priors from deep learning models (e.g., DepthAnythingV2) and robust loss functions to handle noisy pseudo-depths [9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md, 9368-robust-depth-loss.md].

The family has evolved to include confidence-weighted supervision for dynamic scenes [15152-s-nerf-confidence-components.md] and generalized ray supervision for physically based rendering [14127-generalized-ray-supervision.md].

Depth and Geometry Supervision refers to a family of regularization techniques in differentiable volume rendering that incorporate geometric constraints—typically derived from sparse 3D points, monocular depth priors, or multi-view consistency—to resolve the shape-radiance ambiguity inherent in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) [S1, S2].

The claim states that Depth and Geometry Supervision uses geometric constraints to resolve shape-radiance ambiguity in NeRFs. Source [S1] explicitly describes a 'coarse-fine consistency loss' ($L_{cfc}$) that enforces consistency between depth estimates of coarse and fine NeRF models. The text notes that without this consistency, the model suffers from 'blur' and 'floater artifacts' (issues related to shape/radiance ambiguity). The mathematical formula provided in the claim matches the formula in Source [S1] exactly. Therefore, the evidence supports the claim.

The loss is defined as $L_{KL} = \sum_{i}^{N_r} \sum_{t=t_n}^{t_f} D(r_i) - \epsilon \log w_k \exp(-\frac{(t - D(r_i))^2}{2\hat{\sigma}^2}) \Delta t_k$, where $w_k$ are rendering weights, $t_k$ are sampled points, $\Delta t_k$ are distances, $D(r_i)$ is ground truth depth, $\epsilon$ is a kernel parameter, and $\hat{\sigma}$ is a variance parameter [S2].
